vignette:
# Margot

Margot was thirty-nine when she first articulated to a therapist what her husband had been trying to tell her for years: that she was not living a life, but rather a series of careful avoidances. She held the position of City Council Member in a mid-sized northeastern city, a role that demanded presence, visibility, and the willingness to be scrutinized. By all external measures, she was competent—her voting record was consistent, her constituent services efficient, her public speaking composed. But the cost of that composure had begun to show in ways she could no longer rationalize.

The traumatic event itself lived in her memory as fragments, some crystalline and others absent entirely. She was seven years old in her parents' living room in rural Massachusetts. Her father had come home angry—she could see his face, the specific redness of it, the way his hand moved toward her mother's arm. What happened next was a void. She had a clear image of her mother on the kitchen floor, of the sound, but the sequence between her father's anger and her mother's fall was simply gone, as though her mind had erased the footage. She remembered the smell of something spilled, remembered her own small body pressed against the wall, remembered the precise angle of her mother's leg. But the middle—the violence itself—remained inaccessible, no matter how many times she tried to reconstruct it.

Over the decades, this fragmentation had calcified into a particular way of being in the world. Margot had come to believe that danger announced itself through very specific signs, and that if she could only read those signs correctly in other people, she could protect herself. At work, in public meetings, during neighborhood walks, she found herself watching—really watching—the men around her. She monitored the tone of their voices, the tension in their shoulders, the speed of their movements. A colleague's raised voice during a budget discussion would send a spike of electricity through her chest; a man standing too close in a grocery store would trigger a minute recalibration of her body's position, a subtle shift away. She was not conscious of doing this; it had become as automatic as breathing.

The safe places had shrunk over time. Her home was one—specifically the upstairs bedroom she shared with her husband, with the door locked and the curtains drawn. Her office at City Hall, once she had arranged it so that her desk faced the door and no one could approach from behind. A coffee shop three blocks from her house where the owner knew her and where she could sit in the corner. Everywhere else carried a low, persistent hum of threat.

Sleep had become a negotiation with her own mind. She would lie beside her husband, acutely aware of his breathing, monitoring it for changes in rhythm that might signal something. She would drift toward sleep only to jolt awake, her body rigid, sometimes positioned exactly as she had been pressed against that wall thirty-two years ago—a somatic memory her conscious mind could not access but her nervous system had never forgotten. On the worst nights, she would wake gasping, her limbs locked in that child's posture, and it would take her several minutes to remember that she was safe, that she was an adult, that she was in her own bed.

Her husband had suggested therapy two years ago. She had resisted. Last month, after she had cancelled three consecutive city council meetings because the thought of sitting in that chamber—surrounded by people, unable to see everyone, unable to control the space—had made her physically ill, she finally called. What frightened her most was not the memories themselves, but the growing realization that the life she had built was a careful prison she had constructed for herself, and that the bars were getting smaller. She was hoping that someone could help her remember what she could not, or perhaps more importantly, help her stop needing to remember in order to feel like she might survive.
